parts.problem_md:
Some students decided to investigate the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration from leaves. For this, they used a potometer as shown in Fig. 1.

![investigating-transpiration-rates-using-a-potometer](assets/007-investigating-transpiration-rates-using-a-potome.png)

**Fig.1**

They selected a beech tree from the grounds of their school. Beech was selected because it is a species with a thin waxy cuticle.

In the laboratory, they filled a sink with water, placed the small branch underwater and cut a shoot off the branch. This shoot contained ten leaves.

Petroleum jelly (e.g. Vaseline™) was smeared around the edges of the cut end of the shoot prior to inserting the shoot into the potometer, as shown in Fig. 2.

Care was taken to avoid petroleum jelly getting onto the cut end of the shoot.

![cut-end-of-beech-shoot](assets/008-cut-end-of-beech-shoot.png)

**Fig. 2**

(i)

Suggest why a species with a thin waxy cuticle was chosen for this experiment.

[2]

(ii)

Explain why the shoot with ten leaves was cut from the branch under water and not in air.

[2]

(iii)

Explain the purpose of petroleum jelly being smeared on the areas shown in Fig. 2.

[1]

(iv)

Explain why the students should avoid petroleum jelly getting onto the cut end of the shoot as shown in Fig. 2.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) A species with a thin waxy cuticle was chosen for this experiment because:

- (Thin waxy cuticle) will lose water / transpire / evaporate water more quickly (than a thick cuticle); **[1 mark]**
- (So) will produce a measurable result in quicker time / it will be easier to measure its transpiration rate;** [1 mark]**

(ii) The shoot with ten leaves was cut from the branch under water and not in air because:

- Prevents air bubble getting into xylem / vascular bundle; **[1 mark]**
- (Which could) cause an airlock / stop further transpiration; **[1 mark]**

(iii) The purpose of petroleum jelly being smeared on in the areas shown in Fig. 2 is:

- To give a watertight / airtight seal between the shoot and the bung / rest of the potometer; **[1 mark]**

(iv) The students should avoid petroleum jelly getting onto the cut end of the shoot as shown in Fig. 2 because:

- The petroleum jelly would block xylem vessels/tubes / vascular bundle; **[1 mark]**
- (And) transpiration / water uptake is stopped / slowed down; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

**Extract:**

Some students decided to investigate the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration from leaves. For this, they used a potometer as shown in Fig. 1.

They selected a beech tree from the grounds of their school. Beech was selected because it is a species with a thin waxy cuticle.

In the laboratory, they filled a sink with water, placed the small branch underwater and cut a shoot off the branch. This shoot contained ten leaves.

Petroleum jelly (e.g. Vaseline™) was smeared around the edges of the cut end of the shoot prior to inserting the shoot into the potometer, as shown in Fig. 2.

Care was taken to avoid petroleum jelly getting onto the cut end of the shoot.

Before the first experiment, the leaves were dried carefully by blotting excess water from the sink off them using pieces of paper towel.

The students used an electric fan with three speed settings to adjust the speed of air flowing over the leaves. The speed settings were numbered 0 (fan switched off), I (slowest setting), II and III (fastest setting).

At each wind speed they measured the time taken for the air bubble to move a set distance of 50 mm in the potometer.

The capillary tube in the potometer used in this experiment (see Fig. 1) has a diameter of 1mm.

(i)

Calculate the volume of water transpired by the piece of plant in the time taken for the bubble to move a distance of 50mm.

The volume of a cylinder = ***πr***<sup>***2***</sup>***h***, where ***r*** is the radius and ***h*** is the length of capillary tube.

Give your answer in appropriate units.

[3]

(ii)

The piece of beech under zero wind speed conditions took 7 minutes and 45 seconds to move the bubble 50mm.

Calculate the rate of transpiration in mm<sup>3</sup> minute<sup>-1</sup>.

[2]

(iii)

Suggest **two** reasons why the answer you calculated in part (ii) might be an under-estimate of the rate of transpiration that the plant may experience in its natural habitat.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The volume of water transpired by the piece of plant in the time taken for the bubble to move a distance of 50mm is:

- r = 1mm ÷ 2 = 0.5mm; **[1 mark]**
- πr<sup>2</sup>h = π × 0.5<sup>2</sup> × 50 = 39.25 / 39.3 / 39; **[1 mark]**
- Units: mm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

![8-1-1c-atpq---cylinder-volume](assets/010-8-1-1c-atpq-cylinder-volume.png)

(ii) The rate of transpiration in mm<sup>3</sup> min<sup>-1</sup> is calculated as follows:

- 39 (mm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ 7.75; **[1 mark]**

*Allow error carried forward Do not award mark for dividing by 7.45*

- = 5.03 mm<sup>3</sup> min<sup>-1</sup>;** [1 mark]**

*Error carried forward means that if you got sub-part (i) wrong, you won't be penalised twice for that error; if you use whatever answer you gave for part (i) in this calculation, and it works out correctly, then you'll get the ***[2 marks]*** available for sub-part (ii).*

> *It's important to use a decimal number for minutes. 7 minutes and 45 seconds is 7-and-three-quarter minutes which in decimal terms is 7.75. Using 7.45 as your number of minutes only equates to 7 minutes and 27 seconds. *

(iii) Two reasons why the answer calculated in part (ii) might be an under-estimate of the rate of transpiration that the plant may experience in its natural habitat, are:

**Two** from the following:

- The piece of branch is no longer attached to the rest of the tree / it may be dying / stopping its metabolic processes;** [1 mark]**
- The light conditions in the lab may be darker than natural daylight / reduced rate of photosynthesis; **[1 mark]**
- The plant cannot absorb minerals from the potometer; **[1 mark]**

*Ignore, the plant is drying out*

**[Total: 7 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on water uptake in celery stalks.

Water is transported in the xylem tissue in plant stems.

Step 1

One celery stalk was placed into a beaker containing **warm** red stain. Another celery stalk was placed into a beaker containing **cool** red stain.

This is shown in Fig 1.

![cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-1](assets/013-cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-1.png)

**Fig. 1**

Step 2

Both celery stalks were left in the red stain for 10 minutes.

Step 3

After 10 minutes the celery stalks were removed from the red stain.

Step 4

A 5 mm section was cut from the end of the celery stalk which had been in the warm red stain, as shown in Fig. 2.

![cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-2](assets/014-cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-2.png)

**Fig. 2**

Step 5

The section was inspected for the presence of the red stain in the xylem tissue in the celery stalk, as shown in Fig. 3.

![cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-3](assets/015-cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-3.png)

**Fig. 3**

Step 6

If the red stain was visible in the cut section, another 5 mm section was cut and the process repeated until no red stain was visible in the cut section. This allowed the student to estimate how far the red stain had moved up the celery stalk.

Step 7

Steps 4 to 6 were repeated for the celery stalk which had been in the **cool** red stain.

(i)

State **one** safety precaution that should be taken while carrying out this method.

[1]

(ii)

The student’s results are shown in Fig. 4.

![cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-4](assets/016-cie-igcse-2018-paper6-feb-mar-1a-4.png)

**Fig. 4**

Prepare a table and record your results in your table, in the space provided.Your table should include:

- the temperature (cool or warm) of the red stain
- the number of sections that were stained in 10 minutes
- the total distance moved by the red stain in 10 minutes.

[3]

(iii)

Use the data to calculate the rate of movement of the red stain in the celery stalk at each temperature.

Give your answers in mm per minute.

[2]

(iv)

State a conclusion for these results.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Safety precautions that should be taken while carrying out this method include:

Any **one **from the following:

- Cut on a (flat) surface **OR** do not cut in mid-air **OR** do not cut on an uneven/slippery surface;** [1 mark]**
- Cut slowly **OR** cut in a controlled manner **OR **cut only with a sharp blade **OR **cut with a solid/firm/good grip on the celery stalk (and on the knife/scalpel); **[1 mark]**
- Wear gloves / goggles (to avoid stain on body); **[1 mark]**

(ii) The results table should be prepared and completed as follows:

![1e0254d6-58aa-4379-821c-241fda81c8be](assets/017-1e0254d6-58aa-4379-821c-241fda81c8be.jpeg)

(iii) The rate of movement of the red stain in the celery stalk at each temperature should be calculated as follows:

![ba0270d3-475a-4aeb-8a87-b0fb2fc85adb](assets/018-ba0270d3-475a-4aeb-8a87-b0fb2fc85adb.jpeg)

(iv) A suitable conclusion for these results would be:

- The higher temperature, the faster/further the stain/water moves **OR** the lower the temperature, the slower/smaller the distance the stain/water moves;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

> *For parts ii) and iii) be careful and read the information in the question **very carefully** - the question clearly states that "the cutting process was repeated until **no red stain was visible in the cut section**" - this means that the final cut section for each temperature (i.e. the **11th** cut section for the **warm** stain and the **5th** cut section for the **cool** stain) actually contain **no stain**. This means that these sections **should not be counted as 'stained sections' in the results table**, hence **10** stained sections for the **warm** stain and **4** stained sections for the **cool** stain! As we cannot be sure exactly where the stain stopped in the final section, you can give a range of values, as shown in the table.*

parts.problem_md: Which of the following statements about the process of transpiration is correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D.**

- Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, which occurs by diffusion through the stomata

**A** is incorrect as this does not describe transpiration, which is the loss of water vapour from leaves. The movement of water upwards from the roots is known as the transpiration stream.

**B** is incorrect as increasing wind speed increases the rate of transpiration.

**C** is incorrect as water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells, not directly from the stomata.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: water moves upwards from the roots

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: increasing wind speed decreases the rate of transpiration

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: water evaporates directly from the stomata

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: water vapour is lost from the leaves by diffusion

**OR**

- Structure: Cells have lignin (in walls) / walls are impermeable; **[1 mark]**
- Function: (Lignin) prevents collapse **OR **provides waterproofing (of the xylem) / prevents water from escaping; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Structure: (The xylem lumen) is wide / has a large diameter; **[1 mark]**
- Function: (Xylem can) transport large volumes of water; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Structure: (Xylem have) no (cell) contents / cells are empty/dead / hollow pipes/tubes; **[1 mark]**
- Function: (There is) no/little resistance to flow of water / water can flow easily / continuous columns of water can flow / there is no obstruction to water flow; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The role of phloem in plant transport can be explained as follows:

Any **four** from the following:

- (Transport in phloem is called) <u>translocation</u>; **[1 mark]**
- (Phloem) allows bidirectional movement / movement in two directions / movement up or down the plant; **[1 mark]**
- Movement (of food/phloem sap) occurs from a <u>source</u> to a <u>sink</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Sucrose/amino acids/food are produced / taken from storage (tissues/organs) at a <u>source</u>; **[1 mark]**
- A region of respiration/storage/growth is called a <u>sink</u>; **[1 mark]**

This process is known as translocation and will always occur from a source (where the substances are produced / removed from storage tissue) to a sink (any part that requires these products). Some plant organs may be either a source or a sink depending on the development stage of the plant. For example, roots may act as a source during a growth period but become a sink once the growth period is over.*
